cases.suppression: Claimants alleged shootings, beatings and unlawful detention by mine security staff and public and private security forces acting for the mine (Leigh Day).
cases.killed_note: Leigh Day represented families of a number of miners killed on the mine, and four families told AFP their sons were shot dead by security forces; no total was published and the settlement carried no admission of liability, so no deaths are counted here.
cases.conditions: Foreign investment, not a loan: MRM holds an exclusive licence over the ruby deposit, and signs at Nthoro tell residents it is forbidden to farm, build or mine inside the concession (AFP via Mail & Guardian).
cases.title: Montepuez ruby mine: miners and villagers shot, beaten and detained by mine security
cases.place: Montepuez Ruby Mining concession (villages of Nthoro and Namucho), Montepuez district, Cabo Delgado, Mozambique
cases.point: Ruby concession near Namanhumbir, east of Montepuez town (approximate; the sources give no coordinates)

lenders.name: Gemfields (UK), 75% owner of Montepuez Ruby Mining (foreign investor)
lenders.role: London-based Gemfields owns 75% of Montepuez Ruby Mining (MRM); the rest belongs to Mwiriti Limitada, co-owned by army General Raimundo Pachinuapa. MRM won the mining rights to 36,000 hectares in 2011 (AFP via Mail & Guardian; Business and Human Rights Resource Centre).

cases.community: 273 claimants, artisanal ruby miners and villagers from around the mine, alleged in a UK lawsuit that the mine's security forces, including Montepuez Ruby Mining (MRM) employees and public and private security acting for the mine, shot, beat, raped, sexually abused and unlawfully detained them and forced them into menial labour (Leigh Day). Residents of Namucho, a village inside the concession, said representatives of the mining company once burned down the whole village (Leigh Day). In Nthoro, a village of about 12,000 on top of the deposits, residents said gangs, allegedly backed by police, burned homes, and a community leader said police officers and mine security guards did the burning; signs on the road tell residents it is forbidden to farm, build homes or mine inside the concession (AFP via Mail & Guardian).
cases.outcome: On 29 January 2019 Gemfields agreed to pay £5.8 million to settle the claims without admitting liability, set up an independent grievance mechanism and fund agricultural projects of at least £500,000 (Business and Human Rights Resource Centre). Leigh Day said Gemfields recognised that violence had occurred on the mining area (Leigh Day). Gemfields said 105 families would be resettled from Nthoro under a US$10 million project (AFP via Mail & Guardian).

cases.conditions: Foreign investment, not a loan: after construction from 2015, the Kolwezi open-pit copper and cobalt mine resumed production in June 2017 (Amnesty International report).

lenders.name: Zijin Mining Group (China), 72% owner of COMMUS (foreign investor)
lenders.role: COMMUS was set up in 2005 as a joint venture between Gécamines and the Chinese state firm China National Overseas Engineering Corporation; Zijin Mining bought 51% in November 2014 and raised its stake to 72% in 2016, with Gécamines a minority owner (Amnesty International report).

cases.community: Cité Gécamines, home to about 39,000 people with running water and electricity, lost residents as the mine expanded; hundreds were told to leave, some learning of demolition only from red crosses painted on their houses (Amnesty International). COMMUS said 2016 evictees received on average over US$50,000, but residents said this did not buy equivalent housing in Kolwezi; in 2020 a second group of more than 200 households was told it would be evicted (Amnesty International report). Blasting cracked homes (Amnesty International). Mongabay reported that in 2022 40% of the neighbourhood became quarry and 209 households left; protesters said they were offered US$25,000 per household while COMMUS's lawyer said the average was US$80,000, and one evictee said he now pays about US$1 a day for water (Mongabay).
cases.outcome: Residents complained to provincial authorities without result (Amnesty International). COMMUS said its compensation was above market prices and set by the provincial relocation committee (Amnesty International report). Amnesty and IBGDH published their findings in September 2023.

cases.community: Mukumbi, an informal settlement of several thousand people, lay inside the Mutoshi concession (Amnesty International report). The local chief said that in 2015, after Chemaf acquired the concession, three company representatives came with two police officers to tell residents to move, and visited four more times, and that in November 2016 soldiers of the Republican Guard burned houses and beat villagers who resisted; a two-year-old girl was severely burned (Amnesty International). Satellite images show that Mukumbi, about 400 structures including a school, a health facility and a church, was destroyed by 7 November 2016 (Amnesty International).
cases.outcome: After protests, Chemaf agreed in 2019 to pay US$1.5 million through the local authority, but some former residents received as little as US$300 (Amnesty International). Chemaf denies wrongdoing, liability or involvement in the destruction, or directing military forces (Amnesty International).

lenders.role: Metalkol SA, which runs the Metalkol Roan Tailings Reclamation project (operating since 2019), is a company of Eurasian Resources Group, headquartered in Luxembourg with the government of Kazakhstan as its largest shareholder; Amnesty says ERG bought Metalkol nine years before September 2019 (Amnesty International report).

cases.community: Samukonga village, inside the concession, was resettled in 2017, and hundreds of people lost access to nearby farmland; farmers said military officers were present when Metalkol handed out compensation envelopes in September 2018, one receiving US$390 (Amnesty International report). The 144 farmers of Tshamundenda were evicted in 2020: 21 of them said soldiers, some with dogs, occupied the area in February 2020 without notice while their fields were bulldozed, and one woman said three soldiers raped her while she tried to harvest her crops (Amnesty International).
cases.outcome: After protests, the governor of Lualaba wrote to Metalkol in 2020 warning that farmers had not been sufficiently compensated (Amnesty International report). ERG said it had no control over the deployment of soldiers, denied military involvement at Tshamundenda, said it had urged the military to investigate the rape allegation, and said the government had found the 144 farmers were already compensated by a previous mine operator, which the farmers deny (Amnesty International).

lenders.role: Haiyu Mozambique Mining, a subsidiary of China-based Hainan Haiyu Mining, was awarded a concession in 2011 to mine heavy sands such as ilmenite, titanium and zircon (Mail & Guardian).

cases.community: A flash flood on 7 February 2015 destroyed 48 homes and left about 290 people homeless; local authorities recorded 173 more houses partly destroyed (Amnesty International). Satellite images show that by October 2014 about 280,000 m² of wetland north of the village was covered by mining sand and the channel linking the lagoons to the sea was blocked (Amnesty International). The fishing community of about 1,329 people lost drinking water, lagoon fishing, medicinal plants and firewood from the wetland (Amnesty International UK). Later, 1,300 residents moved about a kilometre west of the village (Mail & Guardian article by Amnesty International staff).
cases.outcome: After Amnesty's March 2018 report, the government suspended Haiyu's mining operations (Amnesty International). Haiyu denied responsibility, calling the flood a natural event not seen in 100 years (Amnesty International).

cases.community: Weeks before the reservoir began filling in August 2015, the head of Cipaku village said social impacts on 1,238 households had not been settled and that families had received Rp 29 million for their houses without knowing where to go; the deputy regent admitted the compensation programme was still beset with problems (Jakarta Post via Business and Human Rights Resource Centre). The People's Alliance to Reject the Jatigede Dam said 23 villages were affected, six to be submerged, with 13,092 people including 12,110 farmers, and that of 7,410 households in the six villages only 1,988 were set to be compensated (Jakarta Post opinion piece, citing the alliance). cases.outcome: Presidential Decree No. 1/2015 addressed the dam's social impacts, which critics said did not secure livelihoods (Jakarta Post). Mongabay reported in 2023 that more than 10,000 people have had to relocate for the dam over its history and, citing a BRIN researcher, that many displaced families live below the poverty line.

Tesco, Sainsbury's and Lidl had suspended avocado purchases from Kakuzi in October 2020 (Nation).

cases.conditions: Foreign investment, not a loan: Cerro Matoso S.A. is an open-cut nickel mine and smelter, one of the world's main ferronickel producers (ABColombia).
cases.title: Cerro Matoso nickel mine: court ties illness among neighbouring Zenú and Afro-Colombian communities to the mine
cases.place: Cerro Matoso mine, Montelíbano, Córdoba, Colombia
cases.point: Cerro Matoso mine near Montelíbano, in the Alto San Jorge Zenú reserve (approximate)

lenders.name: BHP Billiton, then South32 (foreign investors)
lenders.role: BHP Billiton held the concession for about 30 years before spinning off South32, which has owned and run the mine since May 2015 (ABColombia).

companies.name: South32
companies.role: Owner of Cerro Matoso since May 2015

cases.community: In ruling T-733 of 2017, Colombia's Constitutional Court found an 'adequate and highly probable' causal link between Cerro Matoso's mining and the illnesses of seven Zenú communities of the Alto San Jorge reserve (Torno Rojo, Bocas de Uré, Puerto Colombia, Pueblo Flecha, Guacarí-La Odisea, Centro América and Puente Uré) and the Afro-Colombian community council of San José de Uré, all near the mine, as well as damage to their water, air, animals and plants (Constitutional Court). A 2016 study by the state's Legal Medicine Institute found elevated nickel in the blood and urine of all patients tested, confirmed by a second analysis by Bogotá's health department; the court rejected the company's claim that the samples were faulty (Constitutional Court). The court also found the company had failed environmental obligations over 35 years of mining and that uncontrolled emissions reached the communities (Constitutional Court). ABColombia reports the illnesses as heart and lung problems, and lawyers represented 3,400 Indigenous people (ABColombia; Blu Radio).
cases.outcome: The ruling ordered prior consultation, a new environmental licence, a state health brigade, and permanent health care paid by the company for residents with listed illnesses including lung cancer, silicosis, chronic lung disease and raised nickel levels (Constitutional Court). In Auto 616 of 20 September 2018 the full court, by 5 votes to 2, annulled the orders for compensation, a special ethno-development fund and possible suspension of mining, but kept the health care, consultation and licence orders (Constitutional Court; Blu Radio). The company had argued the ruling lacked technical and scientific grounds (Asuntos Legales).

cases.community: 71 claimants alleged serious human rights abuses between 2012 and early 2021 by security personnel employed or contracted by the mine and by police working at and around it; ten of the claims came from families of people allegedly killed at the mine (The Citizen; Business and Human Rights Resource Centre). RAID found evidence of 10 killings and 50 injuries of local residents by security personnel since Petra took ownership in 2009 (RAID). The settlement provides medical support including physiotherapy, rehabilitation and psychological care for victims, and lets residents into parts of the mine area to collect firewood and graze animals (The Citizen).
cases.outcome: In 2021 Petra agreed to pay £4.3 million (about Sh14 billion), without admitting liability, covering compensation, legal costs and community programmes, with room for up to 25 more claims and an independent grievance mechanism (The Citizen; Business and Human Rights Resource Centre). Petra replaced Zenith with a new security firm (RAID). Tanzania's deputy minerals minister said Petra settled although the government had not agreed (The Citizen).

cases.title: Patuca III dam: expropriated landowners left waiting for payment and resettlement
cases.place: Patuca III dam, Patuca municipality, Olancho, Honduras

lenders.name: Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC)
lenders.role: US$297.7 million buyer's credit to the state power company ENEE signed on 22 September 2013, with a Honduran sovereign guarantee, for phase 2 (dam wall, reservoir, turbines and transmission), first disbursed on 10 August 2015. Phase 2 cost an estimated US$554.4 million, so ICBC's loan was about 54%; ENEE (US$205.6 million), Bancatlán (US$14.8 million) and Petrocaribe (US$36.1 million) paid the rest. Phase 1, which included land acquisition, was not ICBC-financed (AidData).

cases.community: Land for the project was expropriated from about 400 owners of 12,000 manzanas; by April 2014 the government had paid 317 million of the 1,400 million lempiras it agreed in 2011, to 57 owners (El Heraldo). After the ICBC-financed works began, residents blocked works for 35 days in 2019 demanding land titles, payment for expropriated property and resettlement of families the reservoir would affect: 35 families according to their leader, 15 according to the government project office (La Prensa). In September 2020, after the reservoir had filled, former owners of the land it covers blocked the access road again, saying agreements made since 2011 were unmet, including compensation for the land of 16 families (El Heraldo).
cases.outcome: The dam was inaugurated in January 2021, after delays partly because ENEE struggled to raise US$35 million for resettlement and environmental measures (AidData). The Inter-American Development Bank had declined to finance the project, calling its 2008 environmental assessment too weak, including for failing to consult or compensate affected communities (AidData). The government project office said it was resolving the 2019 demands (La Prensa).
